newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais rescue plan not ready yet.
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais rescue plan not ready yet.

text.p: The rescue plan for Credit Lyonnais is not ready and ideas in a letter from the state-owned bank's chairman, Jean Peyrelevade, do not amount to a rescue plan, finance ministry sources said on Tuesday.
The sources said there was measured backing for some of the main lines of the plan described in the letter, from Peyrelevade to the finance ministry.
Peyrelevade met European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert on Monday to discuss the future rescue plan for the bank -- which will require clearance by Van Miert and his Commission colleagues.

Neither the Commission nor Credit Lyonnais will make any official comment on the content of those discussions but it is the finance ministry which will have to present and agree a final plan with the Commission under standard procedure.
According to sources close to the case, Credit Lyonnais has a series of divestments in mind and is estimating the losses on those sell-offs at about nine billion francs.
The figure frequently touted in the press is that Credit Lyonnais could require a capital injection of around 12 billion francs to get its solvency ratios back to acceptable levels.

The Commission gave the go-ahead on September 26 for emergency 3.9 billion in government aid, which, if added to the estimated nine billion for divestment losses would bring the total above 12 billion.
But it is not clear so far whether Commission and the bank -- the French finance ministry position remains to be seen -- have the same ideas in mind as far as specific divestments are concerned.

French daily Le Monde said on Tuesday the Commission's competition policy staff were keen to see the bank divest from profitable operations as well as non-profitable ones and that the sale of non-profitable operations should be limited in order to limit the amount of compensation sought from the government.
The rescue plan will be the latest of several since the bank ran up huge losses of more than 20 billion francs in the 1992-94 period after runaway expansion in the late 1980s.

Van Miert said after Commission approval of the emergency aid in September that further divestments -- beyond those sought in a rescue package approved in 1995 -- would have to be proportional to the state aid given.
He also said at the time it seemed inevitable that this time round these divestment would have to be carried out inside France as well as beyond French borders.
